title: Pain and Stress Management
introduction: Pain—widely regarded as the fifth vital sign—and stress are universal, subjective experiences that affect physiological, psychological, behavioural, and socio-cultural functioning[cite: 398, 399, 447, 524]. Understanding nociceptive pathways, multidimensional pain assessment, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) stress response, and cognitive-behavioural and pharmacologic interventions equips nurses to deliver individualized, holistic care[cite: 401, 406, 409, 524].
learningOutcomes: 2.1 Define pain, explain its five dimensions, and trace the four physiological processes of nociception (transduction, transmission, perception, and modulation)[cite: 398, 400, 401, 523].
2.2 Classify pain by underlying cause (nociceptive vs. neuropathic) and duration (acute vs. chronic and chronic non-malignant pain)[cite: 404, 405, 406, 523].
2.3 Conduct a comprehensive nursing pain assessment and apply cognitive-behavioural (CBT) and pharmacologic pain management strategies[cite: 406, 407, 409, 410, 523].
2.4 Define stress, stressors, anxiety, and adaptation, and differentiate eustress from distress and the four types of stressors[cite: 447, 448, 449, 524].

2.5 Analyze personal stress mediators (hardiness, Antonovsky's Sense of Coherence, resilience, attitude), the HPA axis neuroendocrine pathway, stress symptoms, and pharmacological and non-pharmacological stress management techniques[cite: 450, 451, 524].

content.heading: Nature, Dimensions, and Mechanism of Pain (Nociception)
content.body: Pain is regarded as the fifth vital sign and is defined by the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) as an unpleasant sensory sensation and emotional experience primarily associated with tissue damage or described in terms of such damage, or both[cite: 398, 523]. Carpenito (1993) describes pain as a state in which a person reports severe discomfort or an uncomfortable sensation; because it is strictly subjective and depends on patient perception, it cannot be measured objectively by laboratory or diagnostic tests (DeLaune & Ladner, 1998)[cite: 398, 523]. Pain spans five dimensions: Physiologic (genetic, anatomic, and physical determinants), Affective (emotional responses like anger, fear, depression, or anxiety that cause suffering; Lewis & Heitkemper, 2007), Cognitive (beliefs, attitudes, memories, and coping strategies), Behavioural (observable signs like facial grimacing, irritability, or agitation), and Socio-cultural (age, gender, education, support systems, and cultural norms, with age and gender also influencing nociception and opioid response; Lewis & Heitkemper, 2012)[cite: 399, 400, 523]. The physiological communication of pain to the central nervous system is called nociception and occurs in four stages: (1) Transduction—naked peripheral nerve endings called nociceptors (Hargrove-Huttel, 2005) respond to thermal, chemical, or mechanical stimuli by releasing hydrogen ions, substance P, ATP, serotonin, histamine, bradykinin, and prostaglandins, generating an action potential carried by fast myelinated A-delta fibres (acute sharp pain) and slow unmyelinated C fibres (blocked peripherally by analgesics or massage); (2) Transmission—the impulse travels via first-order neurons to the spinal dorsal horn (where excitatory transmitters like glutamate, aspartate, and substance P compete with inhibitory GABA, serotonin, and norepinephrine, and where endogenous enkephalins and exogenous opioids bind receptors to produce analgesia), then ascends to the thalamus and cerebral cortex via third-order neurons in the spinothalamic tract (STT) and spinoreticular tract (SRT); (3) Perception—conscious awareness involving the reticular activating system (alerting attention), somatosensory system (localizing/characterizing pain), limbic system (emotional/behavioural responses targeted by distraction and relaxation), and cerebral cortex (constructing meaning); and (4) Modulation—descending brainstem neurons release endogenous opioids in the spinal cord to inhibit pain signals[cite: 401, 402, 403, 408, 523].

content.heading: Classification of Pain
content.body: By underlying cause, pain is classified as Nociceptive or Neuropathic[cite: 404, 523]. Nociceptive pain arises when tissue irritation or actual injury activates pain-sensitive nociceptors; it is generally well-localized, constant, aching or throbbing, time-limited (resolving as tissues heal), and responds well to opioids[cite: 404]. Its subtypes include deep somatic pain (aching/throbbing from bone, joint, muscle, or connective tissue), superficial somatic pain (sharp/prickly from skin, mucous membranes, or subcutaneous tissue), and visceral pain (episodic, poorly localized pain from internal organs)[cite: 404]. Neuropathic pain results from injury or malfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system—such as post-herpetic neuralgia, reflex sympathetic dystrophy/causalgia, cancer pain components, phantom limb pain, entrapment neuropathy (carpal tunnel syndrome), and peripheral neuropathy (most commonly from diabetes, chronic alcohol use, chemotherapy/toxins, or vitamin deficiencies)[cite: 404]. Caused by paroxysmal firing of injured nerves, neuropathic pain feels burning, lancinating, numbing, shooting, stabbing, or electric shock-like, often features persistent allodynia (pain from non-painful stimuli like light touch), responds poorly to opioids alone, and requires adjuvant drugs like tricyclic antidepressants or anti-seizure medications[cite: 405]. By duration, pain is divided into Acute pain (sudden onset lasting less than 3 months, including somatic, visceral, and referred pain) and Chronic/persistent pain (lasting over 3 months, often disabling and linked to anxiety and depression, such as neuralgias, cancer pain, myofascial pain syndrome, hyperesthesia, and chronic non-malignant/benign pain)[cite: 405, 523]. Chronic non-malignant pain occurs almost daily for at least 6 months from a non-life-threatening cause (e.g., low back pain, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylosis), resists available relief methods, and may be lifelong; when severely disabling, it is termed Chronic Intractable Non-Malignant Syndrome[cite: 406, 523].

content.heading: Pain Assessment and Management Strategies
content.body: Because pain is subjective, the patient's self-report is the single most reliable indicator of pain, and nurses must assess eight core elements: (1) Pattern (onset and duration—intermittent, constant, around-the-clock, episodic, procedural, or incidental), (2) Location (precise site, pain maps, and referred pain such as angina radiating to the jaw/left arm or sciatica tracing the sciatic nerve), (3) Intensity (age-specific numeric 0–10 scales, verbal descriptor scales, or pain thermometers), (4) Quality (burning, sharp, shooting), (5) Associated symptoms (anxiety, depression, fatigue, aggravating/alleviating factors), (6) Management strategies (prior prescription/OTC drugs and complementary therapies like heat/cold, herbs, or acupuncture), (7) Impact on functioning and quality of life (sleep, ADLs, mood), and (8) Patient's beliefs, expectations, and treatment goals[cite: 406, 407, 408, 523]. Unrelieved pain adversely affects the respiratory, cardiovascular, urinary, and endocrine systems[cite: 523]. Management combines non-pharmacologic and pharmacologic approaches[cite: 409, 523]. Non-pharmacologic Cognitive Behavioural Interventions (CBT) educate patients and modify attitudes/behaviours alongside medication; they include a trusting nurse-client relationship, distraction, relaxation techniques (imagery, progressive muscle relaxation), biofeedback, cutaneous stimulation (cryotherapy, heat, massage, pressure/vibration to activate endogenous opioids and monoamine analgesia), transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), exercises, and psychotherapy[cite: 409, 523]. Pharmacologic therapy encompasses NSAIDs, non-opioids, opioids, and adjuvant therapies (antidepressants, corticosteroids, anti-seizure drugs, GABA receptor agonists, alpha-2 adrenergic agonists, and local anaesthetics)[cite: 410, 523].

content.heading: Concepts of Stress, Stressors, Anxiety, and Adaptation
content.body: Stress is an internal, subjective, non-specific response of the body to an environmental demand (stressor) perceived as challenging, threatening, or damaging to dynamic balance or equilibrium, typically when demands exceed available coping resources[cite: 447, 524]. Stress takes two forms: Eustress (positive, short-term stress perceived as within coping abilities that feels exciting, motivates, focuses energy, and improves performance) and Distress (negative, short- or long-term stress perceived as outside coping abilities that feels unpleasant, decreases performance, and causes mental or physical illness)[cite: 448, 524]. A stressor is any internal or external situation threatening security and evoking a need to adapt[cite: 449, 524]. By duration, stressors are classified as acute time-limited (e.g., studying for a final exam), chronic intermittent (daily hassles), or chronic enduring (chronic illness, disability, or poverty)[cite: 524]. By source, there are four types of stressors: Physiological (maturation, trauma, illness, poor nutrition, hunger, pain, fear, worry, anger, happiness, abuse/neglect, unemployment), Cognitive (thoughts, perceptions, interpretation, and personal significance of events), Environmental (temperature, air or noise pollution, crowding, time pressure), and Socio-cultural (job or promotion loss, work conditions, and interpersonal conflicts or relationship changes)[cite: 449, 524]. Anxiety is a feeling of dread and apprehension—a psychological response to a threat that can trigger the stress response—whereas Adaptation is the adjustment process maintaining physiological, psychological, socio-cultural, intellectual, and spiritual homeostasis[cite: 449, 452, 524].

content.heading: Factors Mediating Stress Response and Clinical Symptoms
content.body: Four personal characteristics strongly shape how individuals respond to stressors[cite: 450, 524]. Hardiness describes individuals with clear personal values and goals, active environmental engagement, a sense of meaningfulness, and an internal locus of control[cite: 450, 524]. Sense of Coherence (SOC), proposed by Aaron Antonovsky (1979) to explain why some people stay healthy under stress while others become ill, is a global confidence orientation comprising three parameters: Comprehensibility (perceiving internal/external stimuli as ordered, structured, and predictable), Manageability (feeling adequate resources are available to meet demands), and Meaningfulness (viewing demands as challenges worthy of commitment and investment)[cite: 450, 451, 524]. Resilience reflects resourcefulness and flexibility in problem solving, making events seem less stressful[cite: 451, 524]. Attitude reflects optimism versus pessimism, with optimists coping better and experiencing fewer stress-related illnesses[cite: 451, 524]. Unmanaged stress manifests across three symptom domains: Physical symptoms (aches and pains, tachycardia/palpitations, fatigue, distorted sleep/insomnia, headaches, general weakness, anorexia, hypertension, muscle tension/jaw clenching, digestive problems, and sexual difficulties), Psychological symptoms (anxiety, irritability, depression, panic attacks, and sadness), and Behavioural symptoms (reduced activity, loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, and social isolation from family and friends)[cite: 524].

content.heading: Neuroendocrine Stress Pathway (HPA Axis) and Stress Management
content.body: The brain interprets and responds to stress stimuli in six coordinated steps: (1) sensory organs (eyes, ears, nose, skin) and internal baroreceptors/chemoreceptors transmit afferent impulses to the CNS; (2) the hypothalamus and limbic system integrate inputs and regulate autonomic visceral balance; (3) the hypothalamus triggers sympathetic nervous system discharge and activates the sympathetic adrenal-medullary system; (4) persistent stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, wherein the hypothalamus secretes corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), stimulating the pituitary to release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which prompts the adrenal cortex to secrete glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone); (5) glucocorticoids elevate blood glucose for energy and modulate immunity, while aldosterone promotes sodium retention and potassium excretion; and (6) negative feedback loops involving cortisol regulate response intensity and duration to restore homeostasis[cite: 524]. Although no single drug cures stress, symptom-targeted medications include benzodiazepines (Valium, Xanax, lorazepam—enhancing calming GABA signals), beta-blockers (atenolol, propranolol—blocking epinephrine and norepinephrine receptors), and buspirone (regulating dopamine and serotonin to relieve anxiety)[cite: 524]. Effective non-pharmacological stress management techniques include deep breathing exercises, regular exercise (releasing endorphins), mindfulness meditation, sensory grounding techniques, journaling, progressive muscle relaxation, time management, social support, enjoyable self-care, and professional counselling or therapy[cite: 524].

inTextQuestions.question: A 5-year-old boy falls off his bicycle, grabs his wrist, and screams that the pain is sudden and very sharp. Which peripheral nerve fibres transmit this acute sharp pain impulse to the spinal cord?
inTextQuestions.answer: Small, rapidly conducting myelinated A-delta fibres, which carry acute sharp pain signals from peripheral nociceptors to the spinal cord[cite: 401, 408].

inTextQuestions.question: Which dimension of pain addresses emotional responses such as anger, fear, depression, and anxiety?
What is persistent allodynia, and which classification of pain is it commonly associated with?
inTextQuestions.answer: Allodynia is pain resulting from a normally non-painful stimulus such as a light touch, and it is a common characteristic of neuropathic pain[cite: 405].

inTextQuestions.question: Which personal stress-mediating factor was proposed by Aaron Antonovsky (1979) to explain why some people remain healthy under stress while others become ill?
inTextQuestions.answer: Sense of Coherence (SOC), composed of comprehensibility, manageability, and meaningfulness[cite: 450, 451].

saqs.question: Define pain according to the IASP, list its five dimensions, and explain why the patient's self-report is central to pain assessment.
saqs.answer: The IASP defines pain as an unpleasant sensory sensation and emotional experience primarily associated with tissue damage or described in terms of such damage, or both[cite: 398]. Its five dimensions are physiologic, affective, cognitive, behavioural, and socio-cultural[cite: 399, 400]. Because pain is purely subjective and cannot be objectively measured by laboratory tests, the patient's self-report is the single most reliable indicator of the pain experience[cite: 398, 406].

saqs.question: Explain the four physiological processes of nociception (transduction, transmission, perception, and modulation) and identify where opioids and massage act.
saqs.answer: Transduction converts noxious mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimuli into action potentials at peripheral nociceptors via mediators like substance P, bradykinin, and prostaglandins—where analgesics and massage interfere peripherally[cite: 401]. Transmission conducts impulses via A-delta and C fibres to the dorsal horn (where endogenous enkephalins and exogenous opioids bind opioid receptors to block neurotransmitter release) and up the spinothalamic and spinoreticular tracts to the thalamus and cortex[cite: 401, 402, 403]. Perception is conscious recognition involving the RAS, somatosensory system, limbic system, and cortex[cite: 403]. Modulation occurs when descending brainstem neurons release endogenous opioids in the spinal cord to inhibit nociceptive impulses[cite: 403].

saqs.question: Compare nociceptive pain and neuropathic pain in terms of cause, sensory quality, opioid responsiveness, and clinical examples.
saqs.answer: Nociceptive pain arises from tissue irritation or injury activating nociceptors (deep/superficial somatic or visceral), feels localized, aching, throbbing, or sharp, resolves with healing, and responds well to opioids[cite: 404]. Neuropathic pain stems from peripheral or central nervous system injury/malfunction (e.g., diabetic peripheral neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, phantom limb pain, carpal tunnel syndrome), feels burning, shooting, or electric shock-like with allodynia, is often chronic, and responds poorly to opioids alone, requiring adjuvant antidepressants or anti-seizure drugs[cite: 404, 405].

saqs.question: Differentiate between eustress and distress, distinguish stress from adaptation, and explain the three parameters of Antonovsky's Sense of Coherence (SOC).
saqs.answer: Eustress is short-term positive stress perceived as within coping abilities that excites, focuses energy, and improves performance, whereas distress is short- or long-term unpleasant negative stress exceeding coping abilities that impairs performance and health[cite: 448]. Stress is the body's non-specific reaction to a stressor affecting all body systems, whereas adaptation is the adjustment process maintaining physiological, psychological, socio-cultural, intellectual, and spiritual homeostasis[cite: 452]. SOC comprises Comprehensibility (events feel structured and predictable), Manageability (resources are available to cope), and Meaningfulness (demands are challenges worthy of engagement)[cite: 451].

saqs.question: Trace the hormonal pathway of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis during persistent stress and name three classes of medications used to manage stress symptoms.
saqs.answer: During persistent stress, the hypothalamus secretes corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), stimulating the pituitary gland to release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which prompts the adrenal cortex to release glucocorticoids (cortisol, increasing blood glucose and modulating immunity) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone, promoting sodium retention and potassium excretion), regulated by feedback loops[cite: 524]. Three symptom-management drug classes are benzodiazepines (enhancing GABA calming signals), beta-blockers (blocking epinephrine and norepinephrine binding), and buspirone (balancing dopamine and serotonin for anxiety)[cite: 524].
